Q1.answer: The paper addresses the problem that time series forecasting (TSF) systems using standard z-score normalization anchored to training-set statistics (TSD-anchored) become inaccurate when the level of the time series shifts after deployment (level shift / LS), because the normalization statistics become stale and mis-scale inputs.

Q2.answer: Deployed TSF systems encounter level shifts in practice, and the canonical TSD-anchored z-scoring pipeline fails under such distribution shifts, leading to inflated prediction error (MAE).
Q2.missing: Citation placeholders indicate literature support not yet integrated; the paper asserts prevalence but doesn't demonstrate it.

Q3.answer: Existing evaluations confound moment staleness (normalization statistics becoming outdated) with model capacity insufficiency. The paper states these are confounded in the literature they examined and aims to deconfound them via capacity matching.
Q3.missing: The specific literature where this confounding occurs is marked [CITATION NEEDED], so the gap is asserted but not documented.

Q4.answer: They created a synthetic hourly dataset (SynthLoad) with diurnal/hebdomadal patterns and AWGN, injected piecewise constant mean (PCM) level shifts of magnitude s ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8}σ after the training period, and compared three normalization approaches: (1) Baseline — training-set anchored moments (TSD), (2) RWN — rolling window normalization using trailing 48-hour moments, (3) RWN-F — moments frozen after the first post-LS window (ablation). They used a capacity-matched MLP backbone (h=64, L=168, H=24), iso-budget, 5 seeds, measuring MAE mean ± sd on the test period.

Q5.answer: To isolate the effect of moment staleness from model capacity, they used capacity matching (same model architecture for all methods). RWN tests per-window moment re-estimation. RWN-F ablation isolates the adaptive-moment term (continual adaptation) versus one-shot re-estimation at the shift point.

Q6.answer: Experiments on SynthLoad with PCM LS injection at four magnitudes (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8σ). Three normalization methods compared (TSD baseline, RWN, RWN-F). Capacity-matched MLP backbone. 5 random seeds. MAE reported as mean ± sd on test period. IID (no shift) condition also tested.
Q6.missing: Train/validation/test split details, number of periods, and SynthLoad parameter values are not specified.

Q7.answer: IID parity: RWN 0.409 ± 0.007 vs baseline 0.412 ± 0.006. At s=0.6σ: baseline MAE 0.641 → RWN 0.452 (29% reduction). Across s=0.2–0.6σ: 11–29% MAE reduction, sd ≤ 0.012 (seed-stable ordering). At s=0.8σ: RWN 0.712 ± 0.021 vs baseline 0.731 ± 0.015 (~1 sd difference, no clear gain). RWN-F at s=0.6σ: 0.518 (about 2/3 of gain from one-shot re-estimation, 1/3 from adaptivity).

Q8.answer: RWN achieves IID parity (no degradation when no shift). RWN reduces LS-induced MAE inflation for moderate shifts (up to 0.6σ). Most of the gain (2/3) comes from one-shot re-estimation at the first post-LS window, not continual adaptation. At large shifts (0.8σ), RWN doesn't help. Under capacity matching, moment staleness appears to dominate LS error for moderate shifts.

Q9.answer: Generalization to real/non-synthetic data (explicitly stated as open). Generalization to larger backbones (explicitly open). Whether the 48-hour window is optimal (untuned window). Effects of variance shifts or seasonality drift (LS-only tested). Causal claim that moment staleness *is* the dominant factor (capacity was fixed, not varied). Statistical significance of the 0.8σ result (only 'about 1 sd' mentioned).

Q10.answer: Capacity-matched evidence that per-window renormalization (RWN) reduces LS-induced MAE by 11–29% for moderate shifts (≤0.6σ) without harming IID performance, with an ablation showing ~1/3 of the gain comes from continual adaptation vs one-shot re-estimation, and identification of a boundary at 0.8σ where the method stops helping.

Q11.answer: Synthetic data only (SynthLoad). Untuned window size (48-hour trailing window not optimized). Only level shifts tested, no variance or seasonality drift. Capacity was fixed/matched, not varied, so 'moment staleness dominates' is plausible but not proven. Single backbone architecture (MLP). No statistical tests reported (only mean ± sd, 'about 1 sd' for 0.8σ).

Q12.answer: When a time series has a level shift after training, simply re-normalizing each input window using recent data (rolling normalization) can recover most of the lost accuracy for moderate shifts, and most of that benefit comes from just updating the normalization once at the shift point, not from continual adaptation. But this stops working for large shifts (0.8σ+), and it's only been shown on synthetic data with a specific MLP architecture.

The discussion correctly qualifies this ('though capacity was fixed, not varied'), but the abstract does not.
